My question is: From where did you take this unit from Doboj? Where was it when you took them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, at the barracks in Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that police unit arrived up to the Standard building; and from there, you took them to Maricici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And when you brought that unit to Maricici, you said your assignment was to join them to the unit that was already there, to make sure that they are joined?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. They could not be joined because the army was already at Snagovo. But this segment from Maricici to Liplje, that's not where the joining was done. They were just supposed to secure that area; not the upper boundary towards Liplje, but towards Maricici, from that part of the road where you could reach and down towards Snagovo, 50 or 100 metres, and another 50 metres to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You were there when they took control of that part of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa is finished already. So, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My name is Nelson Thayer. We have not met. I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Let me just pick up on a few issues that we left off on. With respect to the Belgrade trial, sir, concerning Mr. Pavlovic, you indicated that you had been interviewed previously by the OTP, I think by somebody named Rita; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when she interviewed you then, she didn't ask you any questions about 1995 or anything related to Srebrenica and the events following Srebrenica, did she?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. But there was a document mentioning both my name and Maric's name, and it was about year 1995, and she said, "I'm not interested in that. I only want to know about 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say you first went to Maricici, how many troops, approximately, did you bring with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know the number. I just know there was one unit of that civilian police, but I didn't know their exact strength. It was not reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just based on the group that you saw, sir, can you provide some kind of estimate? I mean, was it in the range of 50, in the range of 100, more than 100? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly between 50 and 100 men, but I'm not sure even about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say you returned to Maricici the next day and headed towards Snagovo, on that occasion, sir, were you bringing with you any reinforcement, any new forces, on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, I took one number of the soldiers from the brigade who were supposed to link up the civilian police with the forces in Snagovo to go ahead and search the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "brigade," sir, are you referring to Zvornik Brigade soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate approximately how many you say you brought with you that second time when you went towards Maricici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, do you recall whether there were soldiers from any other units; or to the best of your recollection, was it just Zvornik Brigade soldiers that were with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were only from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified earlier today that the only date you can really remember concretely is the 16th of July because you tie that to the opening of the corridor. Did I get that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, that the corridor was still open the next day, the 17th, as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I know it was opened on the 16th, and that date helps me remember earlier dates. And after that, whether it was opened the next day, the 17th, I couldn't tell you because I really don't know. I suppose it was. But those forces continued to pass through because it would have taken more than 15 minutes or an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. You testified that Obrenovic gave you the order to return to Standard from Maricici by radio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And all of your contacts with Commander Pandurevic during this period of time were also by radio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our first -- my first contact with Commander Pandurevic was on the 16th by radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your recollection, did you have any other contacts with Commander Pandurevic while you were in the field in Orahovac before you returned to Standard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my only contact with Commander Pandurevic was when he told me to secure the road from Orahovac to Crni Vrh, and when he said he would send me 60 men from the Bratunac Brigade, and when he also said that any prisoner that we might take must stay at any cost. That was the only contact. And then later, I was ordered to go back to the command, but it was not he who called me to say that; although, it was his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just testified about being interviewed by a lawyer and -- an American lawyer and possibly also a Serb lawyer, who were representing Mr. Obrenovic while he was actively preparing his Defence. I want to ask you some questions about that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 3435 on the screen, please, and we don't have a B/C/S translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you a couple of brief questions based on the English, which we'll have up shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to address the Court if the witness could remove his earphones with respect to this document before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see. Mr. Jovanovic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Could you remove your headphones, please? Mr. Thayer, if anyone of you prefers to have this debate in the complete absence of the witness, I would go for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm comfortable with the witness here, Mr. President. I don't know how long it's going to take. If it's going to take a while, then maybe the witness could use a break. That would be my only suggestion, but I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't got the gift that you were hoping for. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't think it will be very long. I would just like to ask my colleague, because before he uses this document with the witness, this is a double, if not triple, hearsay document that was obtained at a date, where it's absolutely unreliable in terms of information which can be used with this witness. And I would just like my colleague to establish the foundation of this document and to explain to the Court where it comes from, in terms of the dates, before it can be used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A couple of things, Mr. President. First, we've seen my friend himself use numerous documents and anonymous sources in the cross-examination of witnesses, without providing any documentation whatsoever relying purely on his memory and mental notes that seem to be before him. But in this case, what we have done is we have provided the Defence with an information note, an information report, of a conversation between an investigator from the team and the Serb lawyer to whom the witness referred in his prior -- in his earlier testimony during those interviews. And this lawyer took notes which he read to our investigator over the phone. We came up with this idea because in the Popovic team's proofing notes, they indicated that the witness told them that he had been interviewed by the Obrenovic Defence team; and we then, based on that, reached out to the lawyers and tried to get an account of what was discussed during the interview between those lawyers and the witness. We had no idea that he had actually been interviewed by the lawyers for Mr. Obrenovic. And we generated this information report and duly disclosed it to the Defence. They have referred to it, although they didn't show it or explicitly refer to sections, but they have referred to it themselves during the examination. So I see absolutely no basis for this objection. I think we are fully complying with all the practice requirements of the Tribunal, and certainly more than my friend has himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. President, I will not comments on the last part of his statement, which I, of course, fully disagree with. This is simply to say that the lawyer referred to in this conversation is a lawyer -- I think we should go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we left off discussing the interview that you had with the lawyers for Mr. Obrenovic. I just wanted to ask you a couple of questions about what you recall saying during that interview. Do you remember telling the lawyers that, with respect to the Srebrenica operation, that you couldn't tell the precise date when events happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Srebrenica, itself, I really wouldn't be able to tell you the date when things happened in Srebrenica. When it comes to Zvornik, the Zvornik Brigade, and the part around Crni Vrh, Baljkovica, and Snagovo, when I place things around the 16th of July, then I know when things happened. As for Srebrenica, I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall telling the lawyers with respect to the civilian police unit that went to Maricici, do you remember telling the lawyers that you don't remember the exact date that you were asked to go there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, when it comes to the details of the conversation with the American lawyer who represented Dragan Obrenovic, I really can't say that I told him everything that I provided him with all the dates -- details. It had been quite some time ago before that conversation. The only thing I can remember is that I shared some personal things with this American lawyer, told him how I went to school, what school I went to, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you remember telling the lawyers that you don't know who it was that asked you to go?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I didn't say that, because I know exactly who told me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling the lawyers that the next day, when you were called back to Standard, that you didn't know who gave you that instruction to return to Standard?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signalsman of the police told me that I had been requested to return to the Standard, to the command. I didn't know who it was who issued that instruction. I supposed it was the commander, i.e., the Chief of Staff who was standing in for him at the time. Now, who it was who actually picked up the phone over there, I don't know. It could have been the duty operations officer who did it on the instruction of the Chief of Staff. I only know that when I returned to the Standard, I found him there, and he told me to go to it scour the terrain. It was not Dragan Obrenovic personally who spoke to me and instructed me to return, but what I'm saying is that the actual order could not have been issued by anybody else but him. It could have been conveyed by somebody else, by the duty operations officer, but it could only have come from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, then, it would be accurate to say that, as the information we have from the lawyers, that back then you told them that you didn't know who gave you that order to return; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was conveyed to me to return to the barracks, and it is well known who it was who could issue the order to either the duty operations officer or somebody else. It could only have been the commander or the Chief of Staff. Since the commander was not there at the time, it was the Chief of Staff who asked one of the officers to convey the message to me to return to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to object to the last question. I waited for the answer, to be legitimate with my colleague, but my colleague did ask this question already, on lines page 55 lines 21 and 22: "Well, do you remember telling the lawyers that you don't know who it was that asked to you go?" The witness answered the question: "As far as I know, I did not say that, because I know exactly who told me to go there." So my colleague asked the question once again; I let the witness answer. I think that should be the end of the matter, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one more question, sir, with respect to this interview you had: Do you remember telling those lawyers that when you were told to go back to the Maricici and Snagovo area with 60 to 70 men, that you don't know or that you didn't know when you talked to the lawyers who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to object to this because as my colleague has said a while ago, we do not have the statement of the witness to these lawyers. We don't even have the statement of the lawyers. We have the statement made on the basis of an interview with a lawyer and who would have said this. So I don't think the Prosecutor can ask this question in this form, supposing the witness has, indeed, said that. We don't know if he said really that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment to that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just extremely briefly. A, that's been dealt with, with respect to Mr. Bourgon's objection; and, B, it's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We cannot entertain the objection, Madam Fauveau. We are in cross-examination, and you also have to keep in mind that it was not even necessary for the Prosecution to create this document and disclose it or use it. He could have put the questions on the basis of his knowledge, based on the information obtained from this lawyer, and all this wouldn't have arisen. So, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No good deed goes unpunished, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, that's what it amounts to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask the question again: With respect to the interview you had, do you recall telling the lawyers for Mr. Obrenovic that when you were told to go back to the Maricici-Snagovo area with 60 to 70 men, that you didn't know who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the witness answers the question, I'd like to know from the Prosecution whether, by obtaining this information from the lawyer of Dragan Obrenovic, they also did obtain a waiver that he was, in fact, able to give such information to the Prosecution without telling or communicating with his client. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is at this point pure obstruction. It's a silly objection that has absolutely nothing to do with this witness's ability to answer the question that was put to him. I'll be pleased to deal with that outside the presence of the witness when we have some free time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a matter that can be raised in relation to other matters that haven't got a place in these proceedings. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you the question for a third time: Do you recall, when you say you were ordered back to the Maricici-Snagovo area with 60 to 70 men, telling the lawyers for Mr. Obrenovic that you didn't know who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear, but what is not clear is the Maricici-Snagovo bit, but rather from the barracks to Snagovo. Maricici is further than the brigade command which was in the barracks in Karakaj. This is where I received the order to go to Maricici and to link up the line from the police to our forces in Snagovo; and from there, we were supposed to embark on the scouring mission. And I received that order in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me try one more time, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said everything except what you were asked to give as an information. Please pay careful attention to the question that Mr. Thayer is going to put to you and try to answer it with a yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were interviewed by the lawyers for Mr. Obrenovic, and you spoke to them about being sent back to the area of Maricici and Snagovo with 60 to 70 men, do you recall telling those lawyers that you didn't know who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I could have said it, but I don't remember having stated that before those lawyers. I really don't remember that. But I know for sure that the order was issued to me by Dragan Obrenovic, who sent me on this scouring mission, because he was in charge of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's turn to a slightly different topic, sir. You've testified about the dates on which you recall these events happening, and my friends have referred to your state court testimony in the Trbic case, and they have suggested that maybe you got your dates mixed up when you testified there, in fact, a month ago to the day, 19 May. I want to look at some testimony that you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 3434 on the screen, please. We only have an English transcript. We only found out that there was this prior testimony just before the weekend, and were able to crank out the English transcript by the end of the weekend, and that was the best we could do. If we could have page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked a question by the lawyer for Mr. Trbic; and just so it's clear, you were called as a Defence witness, a witness for Mr. Trbic in that trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you were asked the question: "Are you able to recall what happened two or three days before your arrival to Orahovac; namely, on 16th, when you came there?" And your answer was: "Well, of course I can. I received order, I believe on 14th, of the then-chief of brigade, Dragan Obrenovic, to escort the team or the group of either civil or military police officers from Doboj, I believe, to Maricici. So I escorted this group to Maricici; I stayed overnight in Maricici; and the next day, a vehicle came to pick me up. I believe this was on the 15th. Then I set off to get over the group of soldiers through Maricici to Snagovo in order to search the terrain." Further on, you say: "We stayed overnight in one building near the new school in Snagovo; and after that night, I received the order from Dragan Obrenovic to come down to Orahovac together with a group of people." And you continue and you say: "We stayed overnight at Orahovac, and then I got the order to secure the road that I previously mentioned along with those 60 men who arrived." Now, I want to go to page 14, and then I'll ask you a couple of follow-up questions. At the top of the page, the question is: "Okay. So the 60 men from Bratunac, they arrived on the night of the 14th; is that right?" And your answer is: "I don't know when they arrived in Zvornik. I really don't know. But on 14th, evening, people from Doboj arrived and I deployed them to Maricici." And then if we look down at the bottom of this page, you very clearly say: "I know that the commander of those police officers was captured on 15th there at Maricici because there were some combats." Now, sir, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish your question, and then I'll hear Mr. Sarapa after.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, it's clear, is it not, from the testimony you gave in the Trbic case that your recollection of these events is mistaken by an entire day? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer that question. Yes, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the beginning, the statement of my learned friend started with quoting the lawyer: [In English] "What happened was three days before your arrival in Orahovac; namely, on the 16th, when you came there." [Interpretation] Before the witness answers the question, could he be read out from line 13 to line 20, the latter being the beginning of the Prosecutor's quote? And this reads as follows: [In English] "In Orahovac. "And when did you came there on that day. "Well, I would 15th or rather 16th, 16th, approximately." So, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine if he wants to introduce that ambiguity. I mean, I don't have any problem with that being read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have read both pages while they were on the screen and they still are. So I don't think there is any difficulty for the witness to answer the question. And I think what you have raised, Mr. Sarapa, is already answered in the text of these two pages. Mr. Jovanovic, if you could give us your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer, and the answer would be this: On the 16th, I did not arrive in Orahovac. On the 14th, I was on the scouring mission. On the 15th, in the morning, I was at Snagovo. And on the 15th, I set off towards Orahovac around 11.00, 12.00, or 1.00 p.m. That's when I arrived in Orahovac, and I spent one night in Orahovac. Sixty soldiers came from Bratunac on the 16th. And on the 16th, we were about to provide security for the road. They refused to obey that order, and they were returned on the 16th. They could not have been there on the 15th but only on the 16th. And as for myself I could only be there on the 15th in the evening, after which I spent the night in Orahovac. As for the statement, it is possible that I stated the way it has been recorded. But when I read this, I can only tell you that I know exactly how many nights I spent in the field, between the 13th and the 14th, between the 14th and the 15th, and between the 15th and the 16th. And reading this transcript, one might conclude that I spent only two nights in the field, which is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me refocus you away from my friend's question about the 16th, sir, on the testimony that we just heard that you gave about the events in question, and their dates. First, if we look at page 11, you stated there, in answer to the question: "Can you just remind the Court how you received this order deploying you to the field? Did Obrenovic tell you personally, meaning face to face?" And your answer was: "Yes, face to face." "What time was this? "I believe this happened in the early evening, but I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact hours. And then later on, just a few lines down, the question is: "So, all day on 14th up until the evening, you were in the command; isn't that right?" And your answer was: "Yes." So, again, my question to you, sir, is: Based on your testimony in the state court, where you clearly testified that this first order you say you got from Mr. Obrenovic to deploy the troops from Doboj to the Maricici area happened on the night of the 14th, and that is a full day off from what you've testified here today. You are mistaken by an entire day, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I was off by a whole day, but I am claiming this now and I will continue claiming it. On the 16th, when the corridor was opened, I woke up in Orahovac where I had arrived on the previous day, which was the 15th. I spent the night between the 14th and 15th at Snagovo. On the 14th, we went scouring; and on the 13th, I took the police members to Maricici. I can reconstruct all that in view of the date when the corridor was opened and when I received the order from Vinko Pandurevic to secure the road between Orahovac and Crni Vrh. I received that order in the morning, and I could not get to Orahovac in the morning, receive the order, and have people arrive there. What I'm saying now is that I must have misspoke in my previous statement. What I am telling you now is certainly true and correct, and there is no mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just before we break, and that all hangs on your recollection of this date of the 16; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in all fairness to the witness, I used a date and an intercept which is a Prosecution exhibit; and before he puts a question like this to the witness, he should at least take into consideration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Let him answer the question. I anticipated what you were going to say. Mr. Jovanovic, please answer the question that Mr. Thayer put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was about the 16th and whether I am basing my testimony on the 16th and reconstructing the events backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's exactly the question, sir. Is that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I did not understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The question is: Is that what you're doing, basing your recollection, your testimony, as to these dates by working backward from one date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm starting with that one date, and I am working things out backwards in order to reconstruct what was happening to me and what I was doing on the previous days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there. And we have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's put dates aside for the moment. On the first night you say you went to the Maricici area to escort some police forces, where were those police forces from, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how do you know they were from Doboj, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been informed about that. They never identified themselves to me, but that's what I'd been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when were you told this information, sir, that these forces were from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you when exactly. Maybe it was in the barracks; or maybe in Maricici, maybe from them. But I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 3429, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, I don't think that there is a translation in your language for this. There might be. Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise. We do have it. In fact, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S. Do you see about in the middle of the page, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm being told that there is no English. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to tell you. You told the witness that it's not available in his language. It's not available in ours, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have a hard copy in English that I can place on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That would make our life easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, this is a copy of the witness statement that was taken by the Popovic team and signed by yourself back in October of 2007. Now, do you see the portion, sir, where it says: "At around 2000 hours on 13 July 1995," do you see that section, "Dragan Obrenovic assigned me the task of going with a group of soldiers the size of one company in the direction of Maricici village." Do you see where I'm turning your attention to, sir? If we count down, it's the 7th paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You see where it says: "The soldiers who accompanied me were not from Zvornik but from Bijeljina or Prijedor. I do not recall precisely." Do you recall what made you recall at that time in your interview that these troops may have been from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it was it may have been the fact that I didn't know them at all. If they had been soldiers or policemen from Zvornik, they would have known where Maricici was, so I would not have had to take them. Since they were from outside, I had to take them; and, later on, I learned that they were from Doboj. In this statement that I provided to the gentlemen, it is possible, not only is it possible but I did state it as it has been recorded, but I said that I wasn't sure. I only know that they were not from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But I guess what I'm getting at, sir, is you refer to two specific places, Bijeljina and Prijedor, and neither of those locations is particularly close to Doboj. So is it possible that one of the soldiers with whom you had contact during this period of time was, in fact, a police officer from Bijeljina or from Prijedor, and that's why you told the Popovic Defence team that on that occasion last fall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only person I spoke to was their commander. I did not have any exchanges with the other members of the police. When we arrived at Maricici, they were deployed, not the way they were supposed to be deployed because it was night. They were just billeted in some of the facilities, and only the following morning they kind of deployed themselves to their positions. It is possible that somebody was from there, but what I'm saying is that my information is that they were from Doboj, that they were police officers from Doboj. Whether there were people hailing from other areas or other places, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I think you almost answered my question. Let me just try one more time. Is it possible that one of the police officers with whom you had contact told you that he was, in fact, from Bijeljina or Prijedor, and that's why you recalled that in your interview with the Popovic team last fall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt my colleague, but I think this is exactly the same question that it was to the previous one, and I believe the answer was very clear. I don't really feel like saying this in front of the witness, but he said that he spoke only with one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can move to your next question, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3442, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it the case that you can't even say that it's true that the troops you say you were with were, in fact, from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I repeat: I was informed that they were from Doboj, but I can't be a hundred per cent sure of that. I did not inspect any of their IDs. I never checked that. My only duty was to take them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right, sir. I won't even ask you any questions about that document. Sir, have you followed the two prior Srebrenica trials at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. When you ask me if I "followed," are you asking me whether I listened to the transmissions or whether I followed on TV? I watched it maybe a couple of times because not the whole thing was transmitted. It was just reported about only occasionally. The only thing that I followed was when I was -- when I appeared as a witness in Sarajevo. That's when I followed a Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you discussed, during the time period that those trials were going on, these grave accusations in the trials and those events with your friends and former colleagues, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll get back to that in a little while. Now, sir, I'm just going to tell you directly. The reason I'm pressing your recollection about where these police forces were from that you say you recall escorting is that I want to suggest to you that the forces you escorted were actually from Bijeljina, just like you initially thought. I want to explore that possibility with you. So keep that in mind, if you would, when I show you the next couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can we see 3112, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What we have here is a report from Dragomir Vasic. Do you know who he is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who is he, and, more specifically, in 1995, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was, but I know that he was a police member. He was with the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll see later on in this document that he was, in fact, the commander of the Zvornik CJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down a little bit, this is a dispatch dated the 14th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we see here, if we look at paragraph 7, sir, just take a moment. I know it's kind of hard to read. You see the reference to one company of the Doboj: "CJB, PJP, in coordination with Janja SOP, is blocking enemy forces in the village of Maricici, village of Mehmedovici area." You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I think we've all -- everyone here is familiar with what the PJP forces consisted of. The "SOP" abbreviation there, sir, do you know what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know. It's a police abbreviation. That's something that probably referred to one of their stations or units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're right, sir. It refers to a Special Police detachment from Janja. Now, this is dated on the 14th, and this area that's listed here is roughly the area that you say you were in during this period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can we see 65 ter 3432, please -- I'm sorry, that's 916. My apologies. Wait. Sorry, that's -- we have a 65 ter number issue here. Bear with me one moment, please. 916, please -- no, 913.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we have another Vasic dispatch. This is dated the 15th of July. And if we go down to paragraph 3, there is now a reference to two PJP companies from Bijeljina, one company from Doboj, and one platoon of the Zvornik company, and that they are directly guarding the town of Zvornik and fighting the enemy along the Zlijebac-Zlatne Vode-Kula Grad-Maricici line. Now, as of the 14th, we hadn't seen any reference to the Bijeljina police officers in this area, but now we do on the 15th. Is it possible, sir, that this reference to the Bijeljina companies is actually the reference to the troops that you escorted in the night of the 14th and not the 15th -- I mean, not the 13th; and that you were actually with Bijeljina troops on not Doboj troops when you were in this area of Maricici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Maricici, there was that police force from Doboj. I'm saying this again. And what's written here about a company from Bijeljina and Kula Grad, Kula Grad is to the left of Maricici. They were covering that because there were no army troops there. The area that was not covered by the army troops was covered by the centre of public security, Zvornik, with assistance and coordination of other police because they did not have enough personnel to do it themselves. But the unit at Maricici was from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, we see right here in the document that there is a reference to Bijeljina troops also being in this area of Maricici. My question to you is: Are you excluding the possibility that you were, in fact, escorting Bijeljina troops and not Doboj troops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a formal objection. I mean, we can all see what is in this document, and my learned colleague keeps on repeating Bijeljina, Bijeljina, and the very next sentence says one company Doboj. So in order to be fair to the witness, let him see what's inside this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The document is in front of the witness in any case. Yes, Mr. Jovanovic, could you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the previous document, it was written that there was one unit from Doboj, the previous document, when a report was shown from Dragan Vasic of the 14th. This one is of the 15th. I don't know about the report from the 15th because I was at Snagovo. And who was at that time at Kula and Maricici, I didn't know any more. In the previous document, the report of the 14th, it was written forces from Doboj; and this one, as far as I can see, is from the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's exactly my point, sir; and, again, my question was: Even though, as we've already seen, there is a reference to the Doboj troops on the 14th, there is no reference to the Bijeljina troops in that area in that report from the 14th. So my question to you is: Having seen the reference to the Bijeljina troops arriving apparently on the 15th, since they are mentioned there on the 15th, do you exclude the possibility that you were escorting Bijeljina troops and not Doboj troops?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to a new area, sir. You were asked some questions about the late Milan Maric. Do you remember what his position was in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was in the operative section of the brigade. I don't know what exactly he was there, a clerk or something, but he was in the operative section.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you told us a few minutes ago that during the prior trials, emanating from the events following the fall of Srebrenica, that you discussed the trials and the grave accusations that they dealt with, with friends and former colleagues. Was Mr. Maric somebody that you remember talking to about the cases or generally these events, the accusations of what happened after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you frankly, to whom I talked, with Maric or Bojanovic and all those who were in the brigade and the civilians, civilians who were engaged in the brigade, I did talk about investigations, not trials because there were no trials at that time; and I probably spoke about those investigations to Milan Maric as well while he was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just threw out the name of Bojanovic. Is that the same Ljubo Bojanovic that I think you may have testified about earlier in answers to questions from my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Bojanovic, who was a major in the brigade, if that's the one, he, too, is dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. And forgive me if you weren't asked any questions by Mr. Zivanovic about the late Mr. Bojanovic, but I'm going to ask you some questions about him. You threw his name out. So I'm wondering is he another person with whom you discussed the investigations into the events following the fall of Srebrenica with, just as you did with Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand one thing. I remember the two of them, for instance, because we spent a lot of time together, and not only during the war. We knew one another even before, so they remained in my memory. I did talk to other people as well, but these two are the ones I can remember at the moment. If I may say this, I've discussed it also with my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Maric testified in the Blagojevic trial that in the afternoon of June [sic ]13th, Obrenovic ordered him to go to Snagovo, and if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see I misspoke. I meant "July" clearly. My apologies. If we could have 65 ter 3138 on e-court, please, and if we could go to pages 11592 to 93, but starting with 11592.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, it's only in English, so I'm going to read to you some of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are putting it on the screen so people can read along and the translators, interpreters, as well. That's page 51. Q. Now, Mr. Maric testified - and I'm going to quote the transcript, at page 11592, line 10: "That morning, on the 13th of July, a unit assembled. I think it was an ad hoc unit. There were about 25 soldiers from another battalion, about 15 members of the engineering company; then we also had some donors there, 12 to 15; then we had a logistics platoon from our brigade, about 15 to 20 people altogether. And I think that the Chief of Staff ordered them to go to Snagovo sector in order to protect Serbian villages in that area." And if we look at the bottom of the page, he says that: "Later that day, at about 5.00 or 6.00 p.m.," this is continuing on to the next page, "Obrenovic called him to his office and ordered him to go to Snagovo to find that ad hoc unit because," and I'm quoting here, "'Jevtic couldn't really carry out his duties, was unable to organise that. It was obvious that that wasn't a combat unit that had not seen combat before, and that he was experiencing some problems with the unit.'" That's the end of the quote at line 6 of that page. Now, my first question to you, sir, is: Do you recall anything about this ad hoc unit of mixed forces going to Snagovo on that date, the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that on the 14th or the 15th, I got in touch with Maric. It's only then that I learned Maric was up there. And what kind of unit it was, I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we continue a little bit, sir, if we go to page 11596 - we are just waiting for the e-court number - at the bottom, he says: "I met up with Dragan Jevtic in the area of Snagovo on the road. This is where I found them all gathered together in that place. I saw what the problems were," and this continues to the next page, 11597. "And then I deployed the soldiers in such a way that they could defend themselves most effectively. The inhabitants of the village were also there. They were upset, they were afraid. And that evening, I received information that a unit of the special purpose police from Doboj was to come and join up with us. It was to be brought there by Ljubo Bojanovic. So we waited for that unit to arrive."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, 11598, that's page 57 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a question put to Mr. Maric: "That morning or that night, between the 13th and the 14th, did the police from Doboj arrive, and did you link up with them?" And Mr. Maric answered: "Ljubo Bojanovic did bring a group. I think it was between 200 and 250 special purpose policemen from Doboj. And he joined up with us just before dawn. I think it might have been 4.00 a.m. and then we linked up, and this was the area that they -- where they took up positions." He's asked: "That morning or that night just before dawn, did you personally meet Ljubo Bojanovic?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MARIC ANSWERED
utterances.text: "Yes, of course. For them to come along that road from Maricici to avoid any surprises, I took a group of soldiers and went a kilometre, kilometre and a half, ahead to meet them. So I met them personally, and then we brought them back and linked them up with our unit." Sir, my first question is: Are you aware that Mr. Maric has testified to this series of events and his presence in this area with the Doboj troops in great detail?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not aware that he testified; and, second, that group, those special units of the police, those 20 [as interpreted] men that he says went through Maricici didn't go to Snagovo. They could have only passed through the main -- through the old road, Zvornik-Snagovo. I took to Maricici a very small number of men, up to one company strong, max; that is, 40, 50 men, not more. That large group certainly didn't pass through Maricici because on the 13th, on the night of the 13th, I was with those policemen at Maricici. I can tell you for sure that Ljubo Bojanovic didn't know that part of the road. Maybe he knew about it a little, but he never walked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is an error in the transcript, page 77, line 4. When the witness mentioned a group of people, the witness said 200 men, 200 to 250 men, not 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you confirm that, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said [as interpreted] that there were around 220 men from Doboj, in response to what was read out to me from the document. I said that such a large number of men could not have gone through Maricici. However, there is a road, Zvornik-Snagovo; it was a macadam road but usable by vehicles. From Maricici to Snagovo, however, you can only walk, and I assert that Ljubo Bojanovic with all those men did not go through Maricici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe, again, we have one problem with the transcript. From what I heard from the witness, the witness said, "It was read out to me that there were around 220 men," not "I said that there were 220 men."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear because I was looking at the first three lines of that paragraph on page 77, and it's obvious that that is the case. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if we could have 65 ter 3135 on e-court, please, and we will be going to page 43 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Mr. Bojanovic testified in the Blagojevic case as a Defence witness for Dragan --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I really didn't know that, that he testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if there is anybody following with a hard copy, it's page 11710 of the transcript; and in e-court, it's page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at page 22 -- I'm sorry, line 22, the question is -- actually, line 20, the question is: "Where did you spend the night of the 14th?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And our time is almost up, Mr. Thayer. We have only got two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know what? It's probably better just to break for the day, and we will just pick this up tomorrow. I also note that these documents have been admitted pursuant to 92 quater, just so that's clear on the record, but I will not be referring to anything in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jovanovic, we are going to adjourn for today. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. May I just remind you of the advisory that I gave you yesterday not to discuss this with anyone between today and tomorrow. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For planning purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness can leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prosecution had announced one hour, I believe, for cross-examination. Is it possible to know how much time they will take tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, how much longer, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think I think I should be able to streamline; but given some of the cross-examination and some of the, frankly, new issues that were raised in some of the cross-examination, I'm going to need, I think, about 45 minutes tomorrow to finish up. I'll see what I can do to trim what I've got. But there are new areas, frankly, that were raised that we had no notice of in any form or fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You will update us tomorrow morning, and then we will died how to do. But in any case, the next witness needs to be present tomorrow. Thank you. The sitting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
